claim: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) were first discovered in the 1950s.
source: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) were first discovered in the 1950s (Kresge et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kresge et al., 2005

claim: tRNAs play a vital role in the central dogma of molecular biology in all living systems.
source: have since been found to play a vital role in the central dogma of molecular biology in all living systems (Crick, 1970)
evidence: Supported by citation to Crick, 1970

claim: tRNAs were reported in bacteriophages during the 1960s.
source: During the 1960s, tRNAs were also reported in viruses of bacteria (bacteriophages or phages) (Weiss et al., 1968)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 1968

claim: Phage-encoded tRNAs are widespread, especially among virulent phages.
source: We now know that phage-encoded tRNAs are widespread, especially among virulent phages (Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007

claim: The most established hypothesis for phage-encoded tRNAs is codon compensation, where codons rarely used by the host but necessary to the phage are supplemented by phage-encoded tRNAs.
source: The most established being codon compensation, where codons rarely used by the host but necessary to the phage are supplemented by the tRNAs encoded by the phage (Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007

claim: Phages are pushed toward alternative codons as a side effect of differences in the GC content of phage and host.
source: Why phages are pushed toward these alternative codons is generally believed to be a side effect of differences in the GC content of phage and host (Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007; Lucks et al., 2008; Limor-Waisberg et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007; Lucks et al., 2008; Limor-Waisberg et al., 2011

claim: Phage tRNAs may represent a means to counteract the depletion of host tRNAs that occurs as an early response to phage infection.
source: A recent study by Yang et al., 2021 may have hinted at an additional factor: phage tRNAs represent a means to counteract the depletion of host tRNAs that occurs as an early response to phage infection
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2021

claim: The host employs several mechanisms to deplete its tRNA pool, including downregulating tRNA expression, modifying tRNAs to make them unusable for translation, and cleaving tRNAs using anticodon nucleases.
source: The host employs several mechanisms to deplete its tRNA pool, such as downregulating the expression of its tRNAs, modifying tRNAs to make them unusable for translation, and most notably cleaving the tRNAs using anticodon nucleases (Thompson and Parker, 2009; Yang et al., 2021; Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007; Amitsur et al., 1989; Wolfram-Schauerte et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Thompson and Parker, 2009; Yang et al., 2021; Bailly-Bechet et al., 2007; Amitsur et al., 1989; Wolfram-Schauerte et al., 2022

claim: Anticodon nuclease PrrC cleaves tRNA-Lys(ttt) when triggered after sensing phage T4-encoded protein Stp.
source: an exception is anticodon nuclease PrrC, which cleaves tRNA-Lys(ttt) when triggered after sensing phage T4-encoded protein Stp (Kaufmann, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaufmann, 2011

claim: Phage T4 encodes a tRNA ligase that repairs the cleaved tRNA-Lys.
source: In response, phage T4 encodes a tRNA ligase that repairs the cleaved tRNA-Lys (Kaufmann, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaufmann, 2011

claim: A phage-encoded tRNA was found to replenish the depleted host tRNA caused by phage defense system Retron Ec78, thereby preventing the inhibition of phage propagation.
source: Recently, a phage-encoded tRNA was found to replenish the depleted host tRNA caused by phage defense system Retron Ec78 , thereby preventing the inhibition of phage propagation (Azam et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citation to Azam et al., 2023

claim: It remains unclear how phage tRNAs avoid being degraded by the same mechanism that results in the depletion of host tRNAs during phage infection.
source: However, it remains unclear how phage tRNAs avoid being degraded by the same mechanism that results in the depletion of host tRNAs during phage infection
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The tRNAs encoded by phages are insensitive to tRNA anticodon nuclease activity, preventing depletion of the tRNA pool and translation stalling during phage infection.
source: Here, we have analyzed phage-encoded tRNAs and hypothesize that the tRNAs encoded by phages are insensitive to tRNA anticodon nuclease activity, preventing depletion of the tRNA pool and translation stalling during phage infection
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their analysis

claim: Mycobacteriophage cluster C1 contains phages with an average of 33 tRNAs per phage.
source: we analyzed the tRNAs encoded by a large and well-characterized dataset of tRNA-rich bacteriophages (33 tRNAs per phage on average) that infect mycobacteria: mycobacteriophage cluster C1 (Russell and Hatfull, 2017; Figure 1A and B)
evidence: Supported by citation to Russell and Hatfull, 2017 and reference to Figure 1A and B

claim: The bacterial host of mycobacteriophage cluster C1 encodes a range of well-characterized tRNA nucleases, such as VapC, MazF, and RelE.
source: We specifically selected this mycobacteriophage dataset because the bacterial host encodes a range of well-characterized tRNA nucleases (tRNAses), such as VapC, MazF, and RelE (Winther et al., 2016; Chauhan et al., 2022; Cruz et al., 2015; Cintrón et al., 2019; Barth et al., 2021; Pedersen et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Winther et al., 2016; Chauhan et al., 2022; Cruz et al., 2015; Cintrón et al., 2019; Barth et al., 2021; Pedersen et al., 2003

claim: A subset of mycobacterial tRNAses target the tRNA anticodon loop and are activated upon various stress responses, including phage infection.
source: A subset of these tRNAses target the tRNA anticodon loop and are activated upon various stress responses, including phage infection (Calcuttawala et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Calcuttawala et al., 2022

claim: Anticodon nucleases cleave specific tRNAs in conserved regions within the anticodon loop to inactivate the tRNAs and thereby regulate protein translation of the host.
source: Upon activation, these anticodon nucleases cleave specific tRNAs in conserved regions within the anticodon loop to inactivate the tRNAs and thereby regulate protein translation of the host (Winther et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Winther et al., 2016

claim: The cleavage region within the tRNA anticodon loop is sequence-dependent and highly specific to the type of tRNA.
source: The cleavage region within the tRNA anticodon loop is sequence-dependent and highly specific to the type of tRNA
evidence: This is established knowledge about anticodon nucleases

claim: Mutations in the recognition and cleavage sequence within the anticodon loop result in insensitivity to anticodon nucleases.
source: Mutations in the recognition and cleavage sequence within the anticodon loop have been found to result in insensitivity to these anticodon nucleases (Winther et al., 2016; Cruz et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Winther et al., 2016; Cruz et al., 2015

claim: All 10 mycobacteriophage-encoded tRNAs that are targeted by anticodon nucleases contained anticodon loop mutations known to affect cleavage by VapC.
source: We found that all 10 mycobacteriophage-encoded tRNAs that are targeted by anticodon nucleases contained anticodon loop mutations known to affect cleavage by VapC (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a, and Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a, and Supplementary file 1b

claim: Phage-encoded tRNAs are insensitive to cleavage by anticodon nucleases.
source: These findings support the idea that phage-encoded tRNAs are insensitive to cleavage by anticodon nucleases (Figure 1C)
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all 10 targeted phage tRNAs contain mutations known to affect cleavage, as shown in Figure 1C

claim: Phage tRNAs serve as a mechanism to counteract the depletion of tRNAs by anticodon nucleases during phage infection, thereby allowing the phage to translate its proteins and successfully complete the infection cycle.
source: We propose that these phage tRNAs serve as a mechanism to counteract the depletion of tRNAs by anticodon nucleases during phage infection, thereby allowing the phage to translate its proteins and successfully complete the infection cycle (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' findings, illustrated in Figure 1D

claim: Mycobacteriophages rarely encode tRNAs that are cleaved within the anticodon itself.
source: In addition, we observe that mycobacteriophages rarely encode tRNAs that are cleaved within the anticodon itself (Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1b

claim: Phages avoid encoding tRNAs that are cleaved within the anticodon itself, suggesting that no tRNAs evolved to be insensitive to cleavage at these sites.
source: suggesting that these anticodons are avoided by the phage and that no tRNAs evolved to be insensitive to cleavage
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mycobacteriophages rarely encode tRNAs cleaved within the anticodon

claim: Mycobacteriophages avoid encoding serine-coding tRNAs that are cleaved at the GA site within the anticodon (tRNA-Ser(gga), tRNA-Ser(tga), tRNA-Ser(cga), and tRNA-Ser(aga)).
source: Specifically, this avoidance is seen for the serine-coding tRNAs that are cleaved at the GA site within the anticodon (tRNA-Ser(gga), tRNA-Ser(tga), tRNA-Ser(cga), and tRNA-Ser(aga)) (Winther et al., 2016; Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Winther et al., 2016 and data in Supplementary file 1b

claim: The phage encodes a serine tRNA (tRNA-Ser(gct)) that is not targeted by nucleases to compensate for avoiding other serine tRNAs.
source: To compensate for this, the phage encodes a serine tRNA (tRNA-Ser(gct)) that is not targeted by nucleases
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phages avoid certain serine tRNAs but encode an alternative

claim: Mycobacteriophages avoid encoding tRNAs that are known targets of RelE, including stop codon (cta), tRNA-Leu(tta), and tRNA-Gln(cga).
source: We observed the same avoidance for known targets of RelE (Pedersen et al., 2003), including stop codon (cta), tRNA-Leu(tta), and tRNA-Gln(cga) (Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pedersen et al., 2003 and data in Supplementary file 1b

claim: There is no difference in codon frequency between codons for which the phage encodes a tRNA and those for which it does not.
source: when comparing the codon frequency of phage genes, we observed no differences in the codon frequency between codons for which the phage encodes a tRNA and those for which it does not (Welch's two-sample t-test, t = 1.0471, df = 41.591, p-value=0.3011) (Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Welch's two-sample t-test) and data in Supplementary file 1b

claim: There is no difference in codon frequency between phage and host genes.
source: Moreover, we did not observe a difference in the codon frequency between phage and host genes (paired t-test, p-value=0.999) (Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (paired t-test) and data in Supplementary file 1b

claim: In only 2 out of 23 instances the preferred codon of the phage did not match that of the host (tRNA-Val(cac) and tRNA-Ala(cgc)).
source: We also found that in only 2 out of 23 instances the preferred codon (i.e. the most frequently encoded codon per amino acid) of the phage did not match that of the host (tRNA-Val(cac) and tRNA-Ala(cgc)) (Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1b

claim: The phage-encoded tRNAs were likely not selected for codon compensation.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the phage-encoded tRNAs were likely not selected for codon compensation
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations that codon frequencies are similar between phage and host, and preferred codons mostly match

claim: Phage tRNAs in mycobacteria evolved to resist anticodon nucleases in order to overcome host tRNA-depletion strategies that limit phage propagation.
source: Overall, our findings support the hypothesis that phage tRNAs in mycobacteria evolved to resist anticodon nucleases in order to overcome host tRNA-depletion strategies that limit phage propagation
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined observations about mutations and avoidance patterns

claim: Mutations in the anticodon loop near or at the cleavage site of anticodon loop-targeted phage-encoded tRNAs were observed in nearly all instances (9 out of 11) in enterobacteria.
source: Despite this limitation, we observed mutations in the anticodon loop near or at the cleavage site of anticodon loop-targeted phage-encoded tRNAs in nearly all instances (9 out of 11) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c

claim: When the anticodon itself is the target of the anticodon nuclease, as is the case for VapC-LT2 in S. flexneri, the phage generally avoids encoding the target tRNA (tRNA-fMet), except for two instances.
source: When the anticodon itself was the target of the anticodon nuclease, as is the case for VapC-LT2 in S. flexneri, we found that the phage generally avoided encoding the target tRNA (tRNA-fMet), except for two instances
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' analysis of phage tRNAs in enterobacteria

claim: Phage-encoded tRNA-Lys(ttt) in coliphages is repaired by a phage-encoded tRNA-Lys ligase (rnl1 and rnl2) after it has been cleaved by PrrC.
source: One of these is the phage-encoded tRNA-Lys(ttt) in coliphages. In this instance, the phage encodes a tRNA-Lys ligase (rnl1 and rnl2) that repairs tRNA-Lys(ttt) after it has been cleaved by PrrC (Kaufmann, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaufmann, 2011

claim: The cleavage activity of Colicin E5 depends on modifying the wobble position.
source: The cleavage activity of Colicin E5 depends on modifying the wobble position (Ogawa et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ogawa et al., 2006

claim: Wobble position modification might be absent in phage tRNAs targeted by Colicin E5, possibly caused by mutations in the anticodon loop observed for three out of the four targeted tRNAs.
source: which might be absent in these phage tRNAs possibly caused by mutations in the anticodon loop that we observed for three out of the four targeted tRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of mutations in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: Mutations in phage tRNAs targeted by Colicin E5 might affect the recognition by Colicin E5.
source: Alternatively, these mutations might affect the recognition by Colicin E5
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for the observed mutations

claim: The findings in mycobacteria are consistent with almost all (9 out of 11) currently known instances of targeted phage tRNAs in enterobacteria.
source: In summary, our findings in mycobacteria are consistent with almost all (9 out of 11) currently known instances of targeted phage tRNAs in enterobacteria (Supplementary file 1c)
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing findings across different bacterial species, supported by data in Supplementary file 1c

claim: The discrepancies in cases where phage tRNAs are targeted can be accounted for by the presence of tRNA ligases, reliance on tRNA modifications of the cleavage site, or mutations within the uncharacterized recognition site.
source: The discrepancies in these cases can be accounted for by the presence of tRNA ligases, reliance on tRNA modifications of the cleavage site, or mutations within the uncharacterized recognition site
evidence: This is an inference to explain the exceptions to the general pattern

claim: The hypothesis that phage tRNAs evade host defenses may extend beyond mycobacteria and enterobacteria, given the ubiquity of virus-encoded tRNAs and host tRNAses.
source: Thus, we speculate that our hypothesis may be extended beyond mycobacteria and enterobacteria, given the ubiquity of virus-encoded tRNAs and host tRNAses (Ogawa et al., 2006; Cavard and Lazdunski, 1979; Jones et al., 2017)
evidence: This is speculation based on the widespread occurrence of tRNAs and tRNAses, supported by citations

claim: Phage-encoded tRNAs escape targeting by host tRNAses via insensitivity-causing mutations within the tRNA cleavage and recognition site.
source: We propose that phage-encoded tRNAs escape targeting by host tRNAses via insensitivity-causing mutations within the tRNA cleavage and recognition site
evidence: This is the main conclusion/proposal of the study based on the combined evidence

claim: The proposed hypothesis can be helpful in selecting or engineering bacteriophages capable of infecting hosts containing anticodon nucleases.
source: This proposed hypothesis can be helpful in selecting or engineering bacteriophages capable of infecting hosts containing anticodon nucleases
